SE to provide updated quantization config and cost delta estimates

header: Date: 2025-08-11 | Start: 14:30 UTC | Duration: 52m | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
summary: Weekly POC sync to review benchmark results comparing Redwood inference to their baseline provider (VeloxAI). Discussed p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput at 8/16/32 concurrent clients, batching behavior, KV/prefix cache benefits, INT8 quantization impact on tail latency and token cost. Agreed on next steps: share raw traces, run 10k synthetic benchmark with Redwood's batch settings, and follow up on pilot extension pricing.
topics: 1) Results overview vs baseline provider; 2) Tail latency causes and mitigations; 3) Cost per token estimates; 4) Tuning - batching, cache, quantization; 5) Next steps / procurement timeline
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick roll call, then we'll dive into the numbers. Hola, Priya?
[00:10] Priya Narang: Hey Maya, yes here. Evan, Samir, Lara are on too.
[00:18] Diego Ramos: Great. I'll start with the slide notes — apologies if the auto-transcript munges some acronyms.
[00:26] Evan Lowe: No worries, Diego. Excited to see the breakdown. We've been itching to understand the p99 behavior.
[00:34] Diego Ramos: Cool. So high level: across our 1k synthetic runs the Redwood slower tail compared to baseline was actually improved — p50 is about 32ms vs VeloxAI's 40ms for the short prompt tests, p95 about 85ms vs 120ms, and p99 we saw 210ms vs 460ms. Those p99 numbers are noisy but the direction is consistent.
[00:58] Priya Narang: Sorry can you repeat the p99 numbers? I think I missed the last bit.
[01:04] Diego Ramos: Yeah, p99 around two hundred ten milliseconds on Redwood in our lab config, baseline was roughly four hundred sixty. There were two contributors: our continuous batching + KV prefix cache avoided repeated decode work, and the kernel path we selected on the GPU reduced spikes for long context windows.
[01:25] Samir Patel: Did you run that with INT8 quant and the same model weights? We changed quant flags on the baseline side last week and want an apples-to-apples comparison.
[01:33] Diego Ramos: Good call. For the numbers I just gave, both sides used the same FP16 weights; we also benchmarked an INT8 path — with INT8 on Redwood p50 stayed similar, p95 improved about 10-15%, but p99 had mixed results depending on sequence length. For short sequences INT8 helps a lot, for longer with KV cache it's okay but you can get occasional micro-jitters due to quant saturation.
[01:58] Evan Lowe: Hmm, micro-jitters — is that from falling back to a different kernel or from the dequant step?
[02:05] Diego Ramos: Mostly kernel-switching, yes. The runtime sometimes needs a different GEMM kernel when the sequence length changes unpredictably. We're working on smoothing kernel selection which should reduce those spikes.
[02:18] Lara Kim: On cost, how much would INT8 save us per 1M tokens vs the current config?
[02:23] Maya Chen: Short answer: on our pricing matrix, INT8 quant moves the per-token GPU time down roughly 30-40% on the heavy decoder models; that gets you a proportional cost decrease but depends on batch utilization. Diego's team has specific delta numbers in the spreadsheet.
[02:40] Diego Ramos: I'll call out the cost example from sheet: baseline provider cost was about $0.32 per 1k tokens for their dedicated config in these tests; Redwood with FP16 was about $0.26, and with INT8 we saw $0.18 per 1k tokens under stable batching assumptions.
[02:57] Priya Narang: That matches our internal ballpark. Important for us is not just avg cost but worst-case tail hitting SLOs. If INT8 causes p99 to spike, it might not be acceptable for live customers.
[03:10] Diego Ramos: Completely agree. That's why the next test we recommended (and you accepted) is the 10k synthetic run with realish client concurrency to surface tails.
[03:20] Evan Lowe: Quick question on the synthetic load: do you include cold-starts and cache-warm scenarios?
[03:26] Maya Chen: Yes — test plan has three phases: cold-start ramp, steady-state sustained load at target qps, and a burst phase to exercise autoscaling. We also tag requests to analyze prefix cache hit rates.
[03:38] Samir Patel: Are the autoscale thresholds the same as our pilot cluster? We saw some flapping last week when concurrency hit ~75.
[03:44] Diego Ramos: On your pilot we ran aggressive scale-up; that explains the flapping. For production we'd recommend a slightly larger initial pool plus smoothing window on our autoscaler to avoid oscillations.
[03:55] Guest (QA): There's a comment in the doc about batch sizes — what's the recommended batch size for 8 vCPU clients?
[04:02] Diego Ramos: Batch target depends on latency SLO. For 50ms SLO we keep batch sizes low (4-8), for throughput targets we push 32-64. The runtime dynamically forms batches based on queue depth, but you can cap max batch size to prioritize latency.
[04:18] Priya Narang: In your earlier runs where p99 was 210ms, what was the batch distribution?
[04:24] Diego Ramos: Most requests were in small batches (median 6) but some bursts formed 32+; the p99 correlated with those larger transient batches plus a few kernel switches from long history prompts.
[04:36] Evan Lowe: Could we do a per-route policy — keep critical route max batch 8 and background route allow larger?
[04:41] Maya Chen: Yep, per-route policy is supported — you can pin batch caps, route by priority, or route to a cheaper model variant for non-critical traffic.
[04:50] Samir Patel: We got a weird metric on the baseline where the KV cache hit rate was only 12% — are we confident your cache numbers are comparable?
[04:58] Diego Ramos: In our runs the KV/prefix cache hit rate averaged 48% for the test corpus because we reused prompts. But in a more diverse workload it will drop. We'll include the hit-rate distribution in the artifact we share.
[05:10] Priya Narang: Any notes on networking — e.g., if we run private deployment in our VPC, will that affect latency measurably vs Redwood hosted?
[05:18] Diego Ramos: Network delta is usually sub-10ms if VPC peering is in the same region, but if you cross-region or go through extra proxies it can add 20-40ms. For ultra low-latency customers we recommend colocated private nodes.
[05:30] Evan Lowe: On the baseline we saw occasional 600ms spikes; can you point to what might cause that on Redwood?
[05:36] Diego Ramos: Common causes: slow kernel fallback, long GC pauses in containerized stack (rare on our runtime), or an unexpected autoscale event. We'll attach stack traces for the outliers.
[05:47] Lara Kim: Any security/regression notes? We need to show SOC2 artifacts to procurement next week.
[05:52] Maya Chen: I'll drop the SOC2 Type II summary and our recent pen-test report in the share. Also including SSO/SAML and KMS integration docs.
[05:59] Guest (QA): There's some fuzz in the transcript, I heard cube-ernetes earlier — please ignore.
[06:05] Diego Ramos: Haha, yeah the auto-transcript mangled 'Kubernetes' to 'cube-ernetes' earlier.
[06:12] Priya Narang: Practical question: if we pin a model version and you push a kernel optimization, does that change the inference outputs? We have concerns about determinism for QA.
[06:23] Diego Ramos: Good question. Kernel optimizations are purely execution path changes; they don't alter model weights or decoding logic. No change to outputs if we don't change the tokenizer or sampling params. If you pin sampling params and model weights, outputs remain deterministic within RNG seeds.
[06:40] Evan Lowe: Regarding RNG seeds — do you expose deterministic sampling for evaluation runs?
[06:45] Diego Ramos: Yes, for evals you can set a seed and force deterministic decoding. For production traffic by default we leave sampling as configured but you can choose the deterministic mode for regression tests.
[06:56] Maya Chen: Back to the numbers: Diego, can you talk through the graphs on the shared sheet — maybe call out the two spike windows at 11:12 and 11:37 in the trace?
[07:04] Diego Ramos: Sure — window one at 11:12 was a kernel switch: the batch had a long-history prompt that forced the runtime into a slower attention kernel. Window two at 11:37 coincided with an autoscale event where a new worker joined and warmed the cache; the first requests to the new worker were slower until KV warmed. We're adding warmup hooks to reduce that warm cache pain.
[07:28] Samir Patel: Warmup hooks — are those proactive preloads of KV for known prefixes?
[07:32] Diego Ramos: Exactly. When we spin up a new worker we can prefetch top-n prefixes observed in recent traffic to reduce initial latency.
[07:39] Priya Narang: That seems helpful. What about A/B rollouts — if we route 10% of traffic to a new optimized kernel, can we auto-fallback to the old kernel on regression?
[07:48] Diego Ramos: Yes, the rollout system supports canarying and automatic rollback based on rollout metrics (latency, errors, quality signals).
[07:56] Evan Lowe: On quality signals: can we hook Eval scripts to trigger rollback if quality drops?
[08:01] Diego Ramos: We can, via a webhook — when evals report regression beyond threshold we mark the new variant unhealthy and route away. We'll include the eval webhook docs.
[08:12] Lara Kim: A side ask from procurement: will you provide a simple TCO comparison sheet? They want to compare Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs our on-prem numbers.
[08:20] Maya Chen: We'll include a TCO template, with sample inputs for GPU hours, reserved discounts, and expected token volumes.
[08:28] Priya Narang: Great. Anything else on benchmarks?
[08:31] Diego Ramos: One more note: the baseline had a higher variance in throughput when concurrent sessions spiked; Redwood's batching strategy smoothed throughput but at the cost of some median latency lift for certain long-history cases. The tradeoff is configurable per-route.
[08:48] Priya Narang: Can you share the config you used to cap batch sizes? We want to try a cap of 12 for critical paths.
[08:54] Diego Ramos: I'll paste the sample config in the sheet. It's a single field: max_batch_size: 12. Also the request priority tags.
[09:02] Evan Lowe: Technical deep dive question — are KV items stored in-process or shared remote store in your pilot? We saw a big delta if the new worker had to fetch from remote.
[09:11] Diego Ramos: In the pilot it's in-process but backed by a shared snapshot store; warm workers have the in-memory KV and new workers pull snapshot on start. For private deployments we can optionally use a shared high-throughput KV cluster to keep warm state synchronized.
[09:29] Samir Patel: Any estimate on sync cost for a 200GB snapshot?
[09:33] Diego Ramos: It depends on network and throughput, but for 200GB snapshot we typically stream it over 2-4 minutes with compression and parallel transfer in our tooling; effective warm window is ~3-5 minutes in worst case.
[09:46] Priya Narang: Ok that's acceptable. On the SLA question — Maya, can you outline what Redwood proposes for a pilot vs dedicated?
[09:54] Maya Chen: Pilot: best-effort with incident notifications and 99th-ish SLO guidance; Dedicated: SLA-backed uptime and latency targets with credits for breaches. We'll put a pilot extension addendum in the draft contract.
[10:07] Lara Kim: If we agree to a dedicated reserved pool, can we get a billing cap during pilot? Procurement likes an upper bound.
[10:13] Maya Chen: We can propose a capped commitment for the pilot extension period. I'll include a sample cap in the draft pricing.
[10:21] Evan Lowe: Quick thing — can you confirm data retention on logs for the shared traces? We need to redact PHI before sending anything to your drive.
[10:28] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We'll take only perf traces; any payloads are redacted client-side. Diego will include scrubbed traces.
[10:35] Diego Ramos: Noted — we'll scrub tokens and store only timing/stack traces and hashes.
[10:39] Priya Narang: Good. About the 10k run — what metrics will you produce?
[10:44] Diego Ramos: We'll produce p50/p90/p95/p99, throughput curves, batch size distributions, KV hit rates, worker join/leave events, and raw sample traces for outliers.
[10:53] Evan Lowe: Perfect. Any other ask for the 10k run?
[10:56] Diego Ramos: Please run it from your staging region to match network topology; and provide a small sample of your prompt corpus so we can mirror prefix locality.
[11:04] Priya Narang: We'll do that.
[11:06] Guest (QA): Minor note — the transcript keeps dropping 'dd' in 'p99' sometimes.
[11:10] Maya Chen: Noted.
[11:12] Diego Ramos: Last piece — fallback policy. If capacity is constrained we can route to smaller model variants with nearly identical outputs for some use cases. That can cut cost and keep latency bounded.
[11:24] Evan Lowe: Could you quantify "nearly identical"? For our medical summaries we need very high fidelity.
[11:30] Diego Ramos: For summarization models smaller variants may have a slight drop; we'll produce quality delta numbers on the eval harness. For medical summaries we'd recommend keeping critical routes on the largest vetted variant.
[11:43] Priya Narang: OK. Let's recap next steps. Maya?
[11:46] Maya Chen: Recap: Diego uploads artifacts and raw traces; Maya sends pilot pricing and SOC2 docs; Helix runs 10k synthetic benchmark and returns logs; schedule follow-up SLA/legal call. Any changes?
[11:58] Priya Narang: That's right. Thanks all.
[12:02] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in the thread with links.
[12:06] Diego Ramos: Thanks. Bye.
[12:08] Meeting ended.
